notes: Human-graded (blind protocol per runbook). Regulatory content from US public-domain sources; ISO framing from committed corpus maps. Architect-validated.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Snack-food manufacturer in Columbus, Ohio; 120 employees; single plant running two shifts. Situation: The company is installing a new automated packaging line (case erector, powered conveyors, robotic palletizer). Maintenance technicians will clear jams and perform servicing that requires reaching into the equipment, and the line has electrical, pneumatic, and stored mechanical (spring/gravity) energy sources. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Establish an energy control (lockout/tagout) program with machine-specific written energy control procedures for the new line, covering electrical, pneumatic, and stored mechanical energy
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Periodic inspection of each energy control procedure at least annually (1910.147 requirement); include in annual evaluation of compliance with documented evidence

expectedObligations.requirement: Train and designate authorized employees (maintenance) and affected employees (operators) on lockout/tagout; retrain when machines or procedures change
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Verify training records at commissioning and during the annual LOTO procedure inspection

expectedObligations.requirement: Guard machine hazards (points of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts) on the new packaging line
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Pre-startup safety verification before the line runs production, then periodic guarding inspections folded into the annual compliance evaluation

metadata.graderNotes: Complete answer must include 1910.147 with machine-specific procedures AND the annual periodic inspection requirement, plus machine guarding (1910.212). Credit recognition of the minor-servicing exception (routine, repetitive jam clearing during normal production may be exempt from LOTO only if effective alternative protection exists) — a strong answer raises it; a wrong answer asserts all jam clearing is categorically exempt. Mapping must be ISO 45001 6.1.3 (no environmental obligations here); citing ISO 14001 6.1.3 for LOTO is an error. Management-of-change (45001 8.1.3) is acceptable as context but not a substitute for the 6.1.3 register entries. Watch for invented OSHA subsections or citing 29 CFR 1926 (construction) for a general-industry plant.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Metal fabrication shop in Fort Worth, Texas; 45 employees. Situation: Purchasing is introducing a new xylene-based degreasing solvent to replace a citrus-based cleaner. The solvent will be dispensed from 55-gallon drums into smaller wipe-down containers at three workstations. It is flammable and workers will have routine skin/inhalation exposure potential. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Update the written hazard communication program and workplace chemical inventory to add the new solvent
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Verify at introduction (before first use) and in the annual HazCom program audit

expectedObligations.requirement: Obtain the safety data sheet and keep it readily accessible to employees on all shifts
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Check SDS availability at first receipt; spot-check during annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Ensure labels on shipped containers are maintained and that secondary/workstation containers are labeled with product identifier and hazard information
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Workstation labeling walkthrough at rollout, then quarterly area inspections feeding the annual evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Train affected employees on the new chemical hazard before initial exposure (a new hazard introduced into the work area triggers training)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Training records verified before first use; refresher determination at annual evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Store and handle the flammable liquid per OSHA flammable liquids requirements (storage cabinets/quantity limits, ignition source control)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Storage arrangement verified at rollout; monthly housekeeping/fire inspections

expectedObligations.requirement: Make a hazardous waste determination on spent solvent and rags; spent xylene solvent is a listed spent solvent (F003) and likely ignitable (D001), which affects the shop's generator category
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR parts 261 and 262 (RCRA waste determination and generator standards)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Waste determination documented before first disposal; monthly waste-generation tally to confirm generator category

metadata.graderNotes: Must cover the four core HazCom elements (written program/inventory, SDS, labeling incl. secondary containers, training before exposure) plus flammable storage. A complete answer also catches the environmental leg: spent xylene solvent triggers a RCRA waste determination (F003 listing and/or D001 ignitability) mapping to ISO 14001 6.1.3 — this is the discriminator between adequate and strong answers. Watch for: training 'annually' asserted as an OSHA HazCom requirement (OSHA requires it at initial assignment and when new hazards are introduced, not on a fixed annual cycle); invented CFR subsections; missing the dual-standard mapping (this scenario is both 45001 and 14001).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Furniture refinishing company in Macon, Georgia; 30 employees. Situation: The company is adding spray application of solvent-borne lacquers and a two-component polyurethane topcoat (isocyanate hardener) in an existing spray booth. Employees have asked for respirators. No air sampling has been done yet. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Assess employee exposures to the coating components against OSHA permissible exposure limits to determine required controls
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1000 (air contaminants / PELs)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Baseline exposure assessment before or at process startup; re-assess on any coating or process change

expectedObligations.requirement: If respirators are required (or provided beyond voluntary filtering-facepiece use), implement a written respiratory protection program including medical evaluation before fit testing/use, fit testing, training, and program administration
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Program elements verified at startup; fit testing at least annually; periodic program evaluation as required by the standard, rolled into annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Conduct and certify a written PPE hazard assessment for the spray operation (respiratory, skin, eye protection)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: At process introduction; re-certify when coatings or tasks change

expectedObligations.requirement: Meet spray-finishing requirements for booth design, ventilation, ignition control, and residue cleanup
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.107
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Booth verification at startup; monthly booth/filter inspections feeding annual evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Update hazard communication (SDSs, labels, training) for the lacquers and isocyanate hardener
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Before first use; annual HazCom audit

metadata.graderNotes: The trap: employees 'asking for respirators' does not by itself define the obligation — a complete answer sequences it correctly: exposure assessment first (hierarchy of controls, ventilation as primary), then 1910.134 program if respirators are required, with medical evaluation BEFORE fit testing. Voluntary-use provisions (1910.134 Appendix D for voluntary filtering facepieces; a program is still required for voluntary elastomeric use) distinguish strong answers. Isocyanates: most have no OSHA PEL (TDI is an exception) — an answer inventing PEL numbers for HDI should be marked down; referencing the general duty clause (OSH Act 5(a)(1)) for isocyanate sensitization is a plus. Wrong answers to watch: skipping medical evaluation, treating fit testing as one-time, mapping to ISO 14001 (environmental permitting for VOCs is a legitimate bonus mention but was not the dominant ask — credit if raised, don't require).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Distribution company in Allentown, Pennsylvania; 200 employees at a single distribution center. Situation: The company hired a roofing contractor to replace the 30-foot-high flat roof. The contract runs six weeks. The company's own maintenance staff will periodically go onto the roof to escort the contractor and inspect progress, and they also access rooftop HVAC units for routine maintenance year-round. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Contractor's roofing work is construction: fall protection required for employees on walking/working surfaces 6 feet or more above a lower level (with low-slope roof options such as guardrails, personal fall arrest, safety monitoring combinations)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501 (contractor's obligation; host verifies as an 'other requirement')
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Pre-job verification of contractor fall protection plan; weekly site checks during the six-week project; close-out evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Contractor must train its workers on fall hazards and systems used
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.503
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Verify contractor training documentation before mobilization

expectedObligations.requirement: Host's own maintenance employees accessing the roof (escort duties now, HVAC maintenance year-round) fall under general-industry fall protection duties (4-foot threshold; specific provisions for low-slope roof work near edges), not the construction standard
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.28 (general industry walking-working surfaces / duty to have fall protection)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Assess roof-access controls before the project; annual evaluation of rooftop-access procedure compliance

expectedObligations.requirement: Host employer duties on a multi-employer worksite: do not expose own employees to contractor-created hazards; coordinate hazards with the contractor (contractor management as an 'other requirement' in the register)
expectedObligations.source: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) (General Duty Clause) and OSHA multi-employer enforcement policy (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Pre-job coordination documented; weekly coordination checks during the project

metadata.graderNotes: The discriminator is the 1926-vs-1910 split: contractor replacement work is construction (1926.501, 6-ft trigger); the host's own employees doing inspection/maintenance are general industry (1910.28, 4-ft trigger with specific low-slope roof provisions). An answer applying 1926.501 to the host's routine HVAC maintenance, or 1910 to the roofing contractor, has the frameworks confused. Multi-employer/host-contractor coordination should appear (General Duty Clause / contractor management; ISO 45001 8.1.4 procurement is fine as context). All mappings are 45001 6.1.3 — there is no environmental obligation here; inventing one (e.g., stormwater for a roof job) is over-reach unless carefully conditioned on demolition debris practices.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Beverage distributor in Rockford, Illinois; 85 employees. Situation: Yesterday a sit-down counterbalance forklift tipped while turning with an elevated load; the operator was admitted to the hospital overnight for observation and treatment (in-patient admission). The operator was trained three years ago and has had no evaluation since. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Report the in-patient hospitalization to OSHA within 24 hours of learning of it
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.39
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Immediate one-time verification that the report was made and documented; incident-triggered

expectedObligations.requirement: Record the injury on the OSHA 300 log and complete the OSHA 301 incident report within 7 calendar days of learning of the recordable case
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR part 1904 (recordkeeping)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: 7-day completion check; annual 300A summary certified and posted February 1 to April 30; annual recordkeeping audit

expectedObligations.requirement: Refresher training and re-evaluation of the operator: an accident/near-miss triggers refresher training, and every operator must be evaluated at least once every three years
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Post-incident refresher completed before the operator resumes; verify the three-year evaluation cycle for all operators in the annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Determine whether the establishment must electronically submit injury/illness data (size- and industry-dependent under OSHA's electronic reporting rule)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.41
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual applicability check ahead of the March 2 electronic submission deadline

metadata.graderNotes: Must include: 24-hour hospitalization report (1904.39 — 8 hours is for fatalities; answers that say 8 hours for hospitalization are wrong), 300/301 recording within 7 days, and the 1910.178(l) triggers (post-accident refresher + triennial evaluation — the scenario plants an overdue evaluation). The 1904.41 electronic submission item should be raised as an applicability determination, not asserted flatly. Incident investigation itself belongs to ISO 45001 10.2 (a different module/agent) — good answers may note the handoff but the register entries here are the legal reporting/recordkeeping/training duties under 6.1.3. Watch for confusing OSHA reporting with workers' compensation reporting (state obligation, acceptable as an 'other requirement' if labeled as such).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Metal stamping plant in Kenosha, Wisconsin; 150 employees. Situation: A new high-tonnage press line was commissioned. Area noise monitoring in the press bay shows employee full-shift exposures around 88 dBA TWA; the rest of the plant is below 80 dBA. About 25 employees work in the press bay. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Implement a hearing conservation program for employees exposed at or above the 85 dBA (8-hour TWA) action level: noise monitoring, employee notification, audiometric testing (baseline then annual), hearing protectors made available, and annual training
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Baseline audiograms within 6 months of first exposure; annual audiograms with standard threshold shift review; annual training; re-monitor when production or equipment changes alter exposures

expectedObligations.requirement: Because exposures approach the 90 dBA PEL, evaluate feasible engineering and administrative controls for the press line (enclosures, damping, rotation), with hearing protection as the interim/back-up control
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Controls feasibility study at commissioning; progress reviewed at each annual compliance evaluation

metadata.graderNotes: The numeric crux: 88 dBA TWA is above the 85 dBA action level (hearing conservation program mandatory for the 25 press-bay employees) and below the 90 dBA PEL (so mandatory engineering controls are not strictly triggered by the PEL, though good answers still evaluate them; OSHA requires HPD use in specific cases such as employees with standard threshold shifts). Wrong answers: claiming the PEL is exceeded at 88 dBA; requiring the program plant-wide when only the press bay is at/above 85; omitting the 6-month baseline audiogram window or annual audiogram/training cycle. Mapping is 45001 6.1.3 only. Community noise ordinances may be mentioned as an 'other requirement' but are not expected.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Poultry further-processing plant in Wilkesboro, North Carolina; 60 employees. Situation: The company built a below-grade wastewater equalization pit (12 ft deep, hatch access, submerged mixer) ahead of its pretreatment system. Sanitation employees are expected to enter about quarterly to wash down solids and service the mixer. The atmosphere may contain hydrogen sulfide and may be oxygen-deficient. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Evaluate the workplace for permit-required confined spaces; the pit qualifies (limited entry/exit, hazardous atmosphere potential, engulfment/entrapment considerations). Post danger signage and inform exposed employees
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Space evaluation and classification before first entry; re-evaluate when space use or configuration changes

expectedObligations.requirement: Implement a written permit-required confined space program: entry permits, atmospheric testing (oxygen, flammables, H2S), ventilation, attendant, entry supervisor, and rescue/emergency provisions (evaluated rescue capability, not just calling 911)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Program in place before first entry; review canceled permits and the program at least annually (single annual review permitted); per-entry permit verification

expectedObligations.requirement: Isolate the submerged mixer's hazardous energy during entry (lockout/tagout integrated with the entry permit)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-entry LOTO verification; annual LOTO procedure inspection

expectedObligations.requirement: If entries are contracted out instead, host-employer duties still apply: inform the contractor of permit spaces and hazards, coordinate entry operations, and debrief
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 (host/contractor provisions)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-contract verification when entries are outsourced

metadata.graderNotes: Complete answers include: classification as a permit space (not merely a 'confined space'), the full permit program element list with rescue provisions explicitly (rescue is the most-missed element; 'call 911' without evaluating rescuer capability is inadequate), LOTO integration for the mixer, and the annual review using retained permits. The host/contractor duties item shows depth. Wrong answers: treating it as an alternate-procedures space (reclassification requires eliminating the hazardous atmosphere, which continuous H2S potential defeats); mapping to ISO 14001 (the wastewater system is environmental infrastructure but the entry obligations are OH&S). A bonus mention that the pretreatment discharge itself carries environmental obligations (separate register entries) is welcome but not required here.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Custom cabinet shop in Grand Junction, Colorado; currently 8 employees, peaked at 9 employees last calendar year. Situation: The owner attended a trade-association seminar and is confused about which OSHA paperwork obligations apply at this size. The shop has table saws, a small spray-finish corner, and typical wood dust. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register — including obligations that do NOT apply and the basis for non-applicability. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Routine injury/illness recordkeeping (OSHA 300/301/300A) does NOT apply: employers with 10 or fewer employees at all times during the previous calendar year are partially exempt unless notified in writing by OSHA or BLS to keep records
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.1
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Re-verify headcount against the 10-employee threshold each January; register entry flips if peak employment exceeds 10

expectedObligations.requirement: Severe-injury reporting still applies regardless of size: fatalities within 8 hours; in-patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye within 24 hours
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.39
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Event-triggered; verify the reporting procedure exists during the annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: All substantive OSHA standards still apply at any size: hazard communication for finishes/solvents (29 CFR 1910.1200), machine guarding on saws (29 CFR 1910.212), spray finishing (29 CFR 1910.107), PPE hazard assessment (29 CFR 1910.132)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910 (as cited per standard)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual compliance evaluation across applicable standards; guarding checks quarterly

expectedObligations.requirement: Wood dust housekeeping and combustible dust hazard control (no comprehensive OSHA combustible dust standard; enforced via housekeeping provisions and the General Duty Clause)
expectedObligations.source: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) and OSHA housekeeping/ventilation provisions (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly housekeeping inspections; dust accumulation criteria reviewed annually

metadata.graderNotes: This is an applicability-reasoning item. The correct structure: (1) recordkeeping FORMS exempt under 1904.1 based on prior-calendar-year peak ≤10 — with the register retaining the entry as 'evaluated, not applicable, basis documented, re-check trigger defined'; (2) 1904.39 severe-injury reporting NOT exempt; (3) substantive standards apply at any size. Fatal errors: 'OSHA doesn't apply to small businesses' (only some penalty/inspection policies differ); claiming the reporting duty is also exempt; basing the exemption on current headcount instead of previous-calendar-year peak. Credit answers noting the exemption is company-wide (all-times test) and that a BLS/OSHA written notice overrides it. Per the LegalLedger register model, non-applicable obligations stay in the register with applicability rationale — an answer that simply deletes them is incomplete.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Custom metal fabricator in Tulsa, Oklahoma; 55 employees. Situation: The shop is taking on stainless-steel work for food-equipment customers: TIG and MIG welding plus plasma cutting of 304/316 stainless, roughly 20 hours of arc time per day across six welders. Welding on stainless can generate hexavalent chromium fume. Current ventilation is general dilution only. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Perform an initial exposure determination for hexavalent chromium for the welding/cutting tasks; the standard's action level is 2.5 µg/m3 and the PEL is 5 µg/m3 (8-hour TWA)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Initial determination before or promptly at process start; periodic monitoring per the standard when results are at/above the action level; re-determination on process change

expectedObligations.requirement: If exposures are at/above the action level or PEL: engineering controls (local exhaust ventilation), respiratory protection during interim/exceedance periods, regulated-area and hygiene practices, and medical surveillance per the standard's triggers
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1026 (with respirators under 29 CFR 1910.134)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Controls verified at installation; exposure re-monitoring per the standard's schedule; medical surveillance tracked per trigger; annual program evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: General welding, cutting, and brazing requirements: ventilation adequacy, fire prevention, and PPE for welders
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910 subpart Q (welding, cutting and brazing) and 29 CFR 1910.132/1910.133 (PPE, eye/face)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: PPE hazard assessment update at process introduction; quarterly welding-area inspections

expectedObligations.requirement: Update hazard communication for stainless consumables and fume hazards (SDSs, training on Cr(VI) and nickel fume)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Before the new work begins; annual HazCom audit

metadata.graderNotes: The core is 1910.1026 with the correct numbers (AL 2.5 µg/m3, PEL 5 µg/m3) and the exposure-determination-first logic. Strong answers tie ventilation upgrades (LEV/fume extraction) to the finding that general dilution may be insufficient at 20 arc-hours/day, and mention medical surveillance triggers (exposure above the AL for 30+ days/year, among others). Watch for: inventing a specific 'welding fume PEL' citation; skipping straight to respirators without exposure data; missing HazCom. Environmental bonus (not required): welding fume dust collector waste may need a hazardous waste determination (chromium/nickel, potential D007) mapping to ISO 14001 6.1.3 — credit if raised correctly.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: E-commerce fulfillment company headquartered in Reno, Nevada, opening its first California site: a non-climate-controlled warehouse in Fresno, California with 140 employees, including yard workers moving trailers outdoors. Summer indoor temperatures on the mezzanine can exceed 85°F. Ask: The compliance-obligations register was built around federal OSHA. Identify the compliance obligations the California expansion creates or affects. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: California operates an OSHA-approved State Plan (Cal/OSHA); the register for the Fresno site must be re-based on California Title 8 regulations, which are in places more stringent than and different from federal OSHA
expectedObligations.source: Cal/OSHA State Plan; California Code of Regulations, Title 8 (framework entry)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time re-baseline before site opening; ongoing regulatory-change monitoring for Title 8

expectedObligations.requirement: Establish, implement, and maintain a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — a Cal/OSHA requirement with no direct federal equivalent
expectedObligations.source: California 8 CCR 3203
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: IIPP in place at opening; periodic effectiveness review at least annually; inspections per the program

expectedObligations.requirement: Outdoor heat illness prevention for yard workers: water, shade, rest, training, high-heat procedures, and a written plan
expectedObligations.source: California 8 CCR 3395
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Seasonal readiness verification before the high-heat season each year; event-triggered checks on high-heat days

expectedObligations.requirement: Indoor heat illness prevention for the warehouse/mezzanine (California adopted an indoor heat standard effective 2024 with an 82°F trigger and additional controls at higher temperatures)
expectedObligations.source: California indoor heat illness prevention standard, 8 CCR (Title 8; commonly cited as section 3396)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Temperature/heat-index monitoring during warm months; annual plan review

expectedObligations.requirement: Warehouse quota disclosure duties: California law requires large warehouse distribution centers to disclose production quotas and prohibits quotas that prevent meal/rest breaks (applicability depends on statutory employee-count thresholds)
expectedObligations.source: California AB 701 (Labor Code warehouse quota provisions) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Applicability determination at opening; re-evaluate on headcount changes; annual verification of quota disclosures

metadata.graderNotes: The register-architecture point is primary: a state-plan state means the OH&S register cannot simply reuse federal citations — 8 CCR 3203 (IIPP) is the flagship 'no federal equivalent' example and must appear. Outdoor heat (3395) applies to the yard workers; indoor heat applies to the warehouse — an answer covering only one heat standard is incomplete. AB 701 is an 'other requirement' showing register breadth (45001 6.1.3 covers legal AND other requirements); do not penalize absence heavily, but credit it. Wrong answers: applying federal 29 CFR 1910 citations as the operative source in California; claiming Nevada rules follow the company into California. Note for grader: verify the indoor heat standard section number (3396) and AB 701 thresholds independently — the scenario intentionally keeps them descriptive.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Plastics injection molder in Cookeville, Tennessee; 95 direct employees plus 25 temporary production workers supplied by a staffing agency, supervised day-to-day by the company's shift leads. Situation: The temp headcount just doubled for a seasonal ramp, and a temp worker suffered a laceration last week; the staffing agency claims all OSHA duties are theirs. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Record injuries/illnesses of temporary workers whom the host supervises on a day-to-day basis on the HOST's OSHA 300 log (the laceration, if recordable, goes on the company's log, not the agency's)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.31 (covered employees)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Case-by-case recordability determination within 7 days; quarterly reconciliation of temp injuries with the agency; annual recordkeeping audit

expectedObligations.requirement: Provide site-specific and hazard-specific training to temporary workers (machine hazards, HazCom for chemicals in their work areas, emergency procedures); generic agency orientation does not discharge host duties for site hazards
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (HazCom training) and applicable machine-specific standards; joint host/agency responsibility per OSHA's Temporary Worker Initiative (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Training verified before assignment for each temp cohort; quarterly training-records sampling

expectedObligations.requirement: PPE hazard assessment covers temp workers' tasks; required PPE is provided at no cost to the worker (host/agency allocation set by contract, but compliance cannot be contracted away)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: At assignment of each new task type; annual PPE assessment review

expectedObligations.requirement: Define host/agency responsibility split in the staffing contract and treat it as an 'other requirement' in the register (host generally controls site-specific hazards; agency generally handles generic training and workers' comp)
expectedObligations.source: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) and OSHA multi-employer/Temporary Worker Initiative guidance (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Contract review annually and at each staffing-agency change

metadata.graderNotes: The load-bearing fact is 1904.31: day-to-day supervision puts temp injuries on the HOST's 300 log — the agency's claim in the scenario is wrong and the model must say so. Joint responsibility (host = site-specific hazards/training; agency = generic duties) should be framed as shared-but-not-delegable. Wrong answers: accepting the agency's position; putting the laceration on the agency's log; treating temps as outside the OH&S management system scope (ISO 45001 explicitly covers workers not employed by the organization). All mappings 45001 6.1.3.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Grocery distribution center in Tolleson, Arizona; 300 employees. Situation: The company is converting its forklift fleet from propane to electric and building a battery charging/changing area: 40 chargers, a battery-washing station, and lead-acid batteries containing sulfuric acid electrolyte. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Battery charging installations: designated area with facilities for flushing/neutralizing spilled electrolyte, fire protection, protection of charging apparatus from truck damage, and adequate ventilation for gases from charging (hydrogen)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(g)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Design verification before commissioning; monthly area inspections

expectedObligations.requirement: Suitable facilities for quick drenching/flushing of eyes and body where employees may be exposed to corrosive materials (emergency eyewash/shower at the battery area)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.151(c) (with ANSI Z358.1 as the referenced good-practice design/testing benchmark — descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Installed and verified before first use; weekly activation checks per ANSI practice; annual full inspection

expectedObligations.requirement: PPE hazard assessment and provision for battery handling (face shield/goggles, acid-resistant gloves and apron)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132 (and 29 CFR 1910.133 eye/face)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Assessment certified at commissioning; annual review

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazard communication for sulfuric acid electrolyte (SDS, labeling, employee training)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Before first battery servicing; annual HazCom audit

expectedObligations.requirement: Track total on-site sulfuric acid quantity: sulfuric acid is an EPCRA Extremely Hazardous Substance, so aggregate electrolyte across the fleet may trigger emergency-planning and Tier II inventory reporting thresholds
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Sections 302/311/312; EPA 40 CFR parts 355 and 370 (applicability determination)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Quantity determination at fleet conversion; annual inventory reconciliation before the March 1 Tier II deadline

metadata.graderNotes: Must include 1910.178(g) (the specific battery-charging provision — generic 'forklift safety' is not enough), 1910.151(c) eyewash for corrosives, PPE, and HazCom. The differentiator is the environmental leg: aggregated sulfuric acid across a 40-charger fleet can cross EPCRA thresholds (EHS: TPQ 500 lb for emergency planning under Section 302; Tier II reporting threshold for EHSs is the lower of 500 lb or the TPQ) — the expected treatment is an applicability determination with a quantity count, not a flat assertion either way. Watch for: missing hydrogen ventilation; citing lithium-ion requirements (these are lead-acid); mapping everything to 45001 and missing the 14001 entry entirely.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Aerospace coatings and surface-treatment shop in Savannah, Georgia; 70 employees. The shop has been a small quantity generator (SQG) of hazardous waste (spent solvents, paint waste), historically generating about 600 kg/month. Situation: A new defense contract will roughly triple throughput; projected hazardous waste generation is about 1,400 kg/month on a sustained basis starting next quarter. Georgia's EPD administers an authorized RCRA program. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Generator category changes from SQG to Large Quantity Generator (LQG) because sustained generation exceeds 1,000 kg/month; re-notify using the Site Identification Form (EPA Form 8700-12) before operating as an LQG
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 (generator categories and notification; LQG conditions at 40 CFR 262.17)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time re-notification before the category change; monthly generation-rate tracking to confirm category thereafter

expectedObligations.requirement: LQG accumulation conditions replace SQG conditions: 90-day accumulation limit (no 180-day allowance, no 6,000 kg cap alternative), container labeling with accumulation start dates and hazard indication, weekly inspections of central accumulation areas, satellite accumulation rules continue
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR 262.17 (and 40 CFR 262.15 for satellite accumulation)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Weekly documented inspections; monthly verification of accumulation-date compliance; annual comprehensive evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Full written contingency plan and emergency procedures (including submission of a quick reference guide to local emergency responders) and an emergency coordinator — the lighter SQG emergency-preparedness provisions no longer suffice
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 (LQG contingency plan provisions, subpart M)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Plan in place before LQG operations; review/amend on changes in operations, waste, or personnel; annual drill or plan review

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazardous waste personnel training program for facility personnel (classroom or on-the-job, annual review) — a formal LQG requirement
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR 262.17 (incorporating personnel training requirements)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Initial training within six months of assignment; annual refresher; records retained

expectedObligations.requirement: Biennial hazardous waste report (even-numbered years, due March 1) becomes mandatory as an LQG
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR 262.41
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Biennial filing cycle with Q4 data compilation in odd years

expectedObligations.requirement: Continue manifesting all off-site shipments and using registered transporters/designated facilities; note Georgia's authorized state program may impose additional or more stringent requirements
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 subpart B (manifest); state-authorized RCRA program (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-shipment manifest verification; annual review of state program changes

metadata.graderNotes: The crux is recognizing the category flip at >1,000 kg/month sustained, and enumerating what CHANGES at LQG: 90-day clock (vs 180-day), full contingency plan + quick reference guide, formal training, biennial report, weekly inspections. An answer that lists generic hazardous-waste duties without distinguishing SQG-vs-LQG deltas misses the point. Also expected: re-notification via Form 8700-12 BEFORE operating as LQG, and the monthly counting discipline as the ongoing 9.1.2 mechanism. Wrong answers: calling this 'episodic generation' (it is a sustained change, so episodic provisions do not preserve SQG status); using 2,200 lb/1,000 kg interchangeably without noting the regulatory threshold is 1,000 kg; forgetting state authorization. Mapping is ISO 14001 6.1.3 throughout (worker training on hazardous waste handling may also be cross-referenced to 45001 — acceptable, not required).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Regional trucking terminal outside Billings, Montana; 40 employees. Situation: The company is installing a 2,000-gallon aboveground diesel tank for fleet fueling. Existing oil storage: a 500-gallon used-oil tank, a 275-gallon heating-oil tote, and four 55-gallon drums of lube oil. A drainage ditch at the property line connects to a creek. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Prepare and implement an SPCC plan: aggregate aboveground oil storage capacity (counting only containers of 55 gallons or more: 2,000 + 500 + 275 + 220 = 2,995 gallons) now exceeds the 1,320-gallon threshold, and the ditch-to-creek pathway supports a reasonable expectation of discharge to navigable waters
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (SPCC)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Plan prepared before the new tank enters service; plan review at least every five years; amend on facility changes

expectedObligations.requirement: The facility likely qualifies as a Tier I qualified facility (≤10,000 gallons aggregate and no single container above 5,000 gallons, absent disqualifying discharge history), allowing owner self-certification of the plan instead of a Professional Engineer certification
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (qualified facility provisions)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Eligibility re-verified whenever storage capacity changes

expectedObligations.requirement: Implement the plan's operational controls: secondary containment/diversionary measures, tank and container inspections, security, loading/unloading procedures for fuel deliveries, and discharge response provisions
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (as implemented in the facility SPCC plan)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Routine visual inspections on the schedule set by the plan (typically monthly); records retained

expectedObligations.requirement: Annual discharge prevention briefings/training for oil-handling personnel
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (training/briefing provisions)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annually, with records; verify in annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Used-oil management standards continue to apply to the 500-gallon used-oil tank (labeling 'Used Oil', container condition, release response)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 279
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly area inspection; annual evaluation

metadata.graderNotes: Scoring hinges on the arithmetic and counting rules: only containers ≥55 gallons count; the four drums count (220 gal); total 2,995 gal exceeds 1,320 gal — the NEW tank is what crosses the threshold. The 'reasonable expectation of discharge to navigable waters' element must be addressed (the ditch/creek supplies it), not assumed silently. Tier I self-certification eligibility (≤10,000 aggregate, no container >5,000 gal) is the depth marker — requiring a PE certification without discussing qualified-facility status is a common wrong answer. Other errors: counting the drums out (they are exactly 55 gal, so they count); including containers under 55 gallons; claiming underground thresholds (42,000 gal) apply to ASTs. All mappings ISO 14001 6.1.3.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Beverage bottling plant in Olathe, Kansas; 110 employees. Situation: After a fleet and equipment expansion, a year-end inventory shows: 14,000 pounds of propane on site for fleet fueling and heaters, and about 900 pounds of sulfuric acid contained in forklift and UPS batteries. Neither chemical previously exceeded any reporting threshold. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register — including any thresholds that are NOT crossed. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Annual Tier II hazardous chemical inventory report due March 1 covering propane (a hazardous chemical present above the 10,000-pound threshold) and sulfuric acid (an Extremely Hazardous Substance present above its Tier II threshold — the lower of 500 pounds or its TPQ)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 312; EPA 40 CFR part 370
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual inventory reconciliation in Q4; file by March 1; re-evaluate at any significant inventory change

expectedObligations.requirement: One-time submission of SDSs or a chemical list to the SERC/TERC, LEPC, and fire department within 90 days of first exceeding a threshold
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 311; EPA 40 CFR part 370
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time, within 90 days of the threshold exceedance; update on new chemicals or significant changes

expectedObligations.requirement: EPCRA Section 302 emergency-planning notification is NOT triggered: sulfuric acid's Threshold Planning Quantity is 1,000 pounds and only about 900 pounds is present; register the obligation as evaluated-not-applicable with a re-check trigger tied to battery-fleet growth
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 302; EPA 40 CFR part 355
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Re-verify against the 1,000-pound TPQ at each inventory change and annually

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazard communication and PPE for employees handling battery electrolyte and propane (existing obligations affected by the larger quantities)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual HazCom audit; PPE assessment review at change

metadata.graderNotes: This is a three-threshold discrimination test: (1) propane at 14,000 lb exceeds the 10,000 lb Tier II threshold for ordinary hazardous chemicals — reportable; (2) sulfuric acid is an EHS, so its Tier II threshold is 500 lb (lower of 500 or TPQ) — 900 lb is reportable; (3) Section 302 emergency planning needs the full TPQ (1,000 lb for sulfuric acid) — 900 lb does NOT trigger it. An answer must get all three directions right; the most common failure is collapsing Tier II and 302 into one threshold. Also expected: the 311 one-time SDS/list submission with the 90-day clock — frequently forgotten. Credit answers that note state/local Tier II fees or portals descriptively. Watch for: 'batteries are exempt' claims (EPA's position is that sulfuric acid in batteries generally counts for EPCRA inventory purposes — the scenario is built on that premise); inventing a propane exemption.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Scrap metal recycler in Pasadena, Texas; 35 employees. Situation: The company is opening a new 4-acre outdoor yard for receiving, sorting, shearing, and staging ferrous and nonferrous scrap. Rainfall runs off the yard to a municipal storm drain. Texas (TCEQ) administers the NPDES program (TPDES). Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Obtain industrial stormwater discharge permit coverage before discharging: scrap recycling is a regulated industrial activity; in Texas this means coverage under the TCEQ Multi-Sector General Permit (file a Notice of Intent) or an individual permit
expectedObligations.source: Clean Water Act NPDES program; EPA 40 CFR 122.26 (industrial stormwater); TCEQ TPDES Multi-Sector General Permit (state-administered)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: NOI filed and coverage confirmed before yard operations begin; permit renewal per the general permit cycle

expectedObligations.requirement: Develop and implement a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) with best management practices for scrap handling (fluid-bearing scrap acceptance procedures, containment, housekeeping)
expectedObligations.source: Multi-Sector General Permit conditions (scrap recycling sector) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: SWPPP complete before operations; update on facility or BMP changes; annual comprehensive review

expectedObligations.requirement: Conduct the permit's monitoring regime: routine facility inspections, quarterly visual assessments of stormwater discharges, and sector benchmark analytical monitoring (metals are typical benchmarks for scrap recycling)
expectedObligations.source: Multi-Sector General Permit monitoring conditions — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Quarterly visual assessments and benchmark sampling per permit schedule; annual comprehensive site inspection; exceedance-triggered corrective action review

expectedObligations.requirement: The conditional 'no exposure' exclusion is NOT available: scrap processing and storage are outdoors and exposed to precipitation; register as evaluated-not-applicable with the basis documented
expectedObligations.source: EPA stormwater no-exposure exclusion provisions (40 CFR 122.26) — applicability determination
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Re-evaluate only if operations are fully enclosed in the future

metadata.graderNotes: Required: permit coverage BEFORE discharge (NOI timing), SWPPP, and the monitoring cadence (quarterly visual + benchmark monitoring + routine inspections) — the cadence is exactly what feeds ISO 9.1.2, so a vague 'monitor stormwater' answer is weak. The state-administration point matters: Texas TPDES, not EPA, issues the permit here; an answer directing the company to EPA's federal MSGP misunderstands NPDES delegation. The no-exposure exclusion should be raised and correctly rejected. Watch for: confusing the construction general permit (for building the yard, if ≥1 acre is disturbed — actually a legitimate bonus obligation during construction; credit it) with the industrial MSGP for operations; inventing numeric effluent limits (benchmarks are not effluent limits).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Regional grocery chain headquartered in Ocala, Florida; 22 stores; in-house refrigeration technicians. Situation: The chain runs rack refrigeration systems with typical charges of 300-500 pounds of R-448A (an HFC blend) per store, and is planning remodels that will modify several systems. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Technicians who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of appliances must hold EPA Section 608 technician certification; refrigerant sales restrictions and required recovery/evacuation practices apply to service work
expectedObligations.source: Clean Air Act Section 608; EPA 40 CFR part 82, subpart F
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Certification verified at hire and tracked in the register; annual roster review

expectedObligations.requirement: Refrigerant leak-management duties for large appliances: calculate leak rates when refrigerant is added, repair leaks above the applicable threshold within the required period (30 days as the general rule), with follow-up verification, and retrofit/retirement planning when repairs fail; EPA's AIM Act emissions-reduction rulemaking extends appliance leak-repair obligations to HFC systems
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 82, subpart F, and EPA regulations under the AIM Act (40 CFR part 84) — describe; compliance dates and charge-size triggers per the current rules
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Leak-rate calculation at every refrigerant addition; monthly review of open leak repairs; annual program evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Service, leak-inspection, and refrigerant purchase/disposition recordkeeping for each system, retained per the applicable retention periods
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 82, subpart F (and AIM Act rules for HFC appliances) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-service-event records; quarterly completeness audit

expectedObligations.requirement: HFC phasedown planning: R-448A components are subject to the AIM Act HFC phasedown and technology-transition restrictions, affecting refrigerant availability/price and the remodel design choices
expectedObligations.source: AIM Act; EPA 40 CFR part 84 (phasedown and technology transitions) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual regulatory-change review feeding remodel/refrigerant strategy; register update on each EPA rule milestone

metadata.graderNotes: Historically, Section 608 leak-repair applied to ozone-depleting refrigerants, and EPA's application to HFC-only appliances has shifted across rulemakings (2016 extension, 2020 partial rollback, and AIM Act-based reinstatement with a lower charge threshold). The eval intentionally requires only the descriptive shape: certified techs, leak-rate calculation on every charge addition, threshold-triggered repair deadlines (30-day general rule), records, and AIM Act phasedown awareness. Grader should verify current charge-size triggers and leak-rate percentages independently and NOT penalize a model for reasonable, hedged statements of them — but SHOULD penalize confidently wrong specifics (e.g., claiming HFC systems are wholly unregulated, or inventing thresholds). Technician certification (608) and recovery requirements are firm and must appear. OH&S bonus: ammonia is absent here — a model adding PSM/RMP obligations for HFC racks is over-applying (neither lists R-448A).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Fleet maintenance garage in Springfield, Missouri; 25 employees; services a municipal-contract bus and truck fleet. Situation: A compliance review found: used motor oil stored in a 300-gallon tank, spent fluorescent lamps boxed in a corner for over a year, a shelf of used aerosol cans, drained oil filters in a drum, and a solvent parts washer whose spent solvent has never had a waste determination. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Manage used oil under the used-oil standards: containers/tanks in good condition, labeled 'Used Oil', releases cleaned up, and off-site shipment via a transporter with an EPA ID number (used oil destined for recycling is not managed as hazardous waste)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 279
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly storage-area inspection; per-shipment transporter verification

expectedObligations.requirement: Manage spent fluorescent lamps, batteries, and (in most states) aerosol cans as universal waste: labeled containers, closed/structurally sound, accumulation limited to one year, employee awareness training — the year-old lamp boxes are at/over the accumulation limit and must ship
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 273 (universal waste)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Accumulation-date tracking monthly; ship before the one-year limit; annual training refresh

expectedObligations.requirement: Complete a hazardous waste determination for the spent parts-washer solvent (potentially an F-listed spent solvent and/or ignitable D001) — an unconditional generator duty that has not been met
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 (waste determination duty; listings/characteristics at 40 CFR part 261)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Immediate determination; re-determine on solvent or process change; documentation retained

expectedObligations.requirement: Establish the facility's generator category by counting all hazardous waste generated per month (likely VSQG at this scale: up to 100 kg/month, with conditional exemptions but still requiring proper waste handling and delivery to an authorized facility)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 (generator categories; VSQG conditions at 40 CFR 262.14)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly generation counting; annual category confirmation

expectedObligations.requirement: Manage drained used oil filters per the applicable exclusion (properly gravity-drained filters are generally excluded from hazardous waste) and per any more-stringent state requirements
expectedObligations.source: EPA used oil filter exclusion (descriptive; state program may vary)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Practice verified in monthly inspections

metadata.graderNotes: The scenario plants a violation (lamps over the one-year universal-waste limit) and an unmet unconditional duty (no waste determination on the solvent) — a complete answer flags both as current non-compliances feeding the CAPA handoff, not just future obligations. The used-oil/hazardous-waste boundary (part 279 vs part 262) is the conceptual test: used oil recycled is NOT hazardous waste; spent solvent very likely IS regulated. Watch for: 'aerosols are trash' (they are universal waste federally since 2019, state adoption varies — descriptive treatment fine); ignoring generator-category counting; over-prescribing LQG-style requirements for a garage that is plausibly VSQG. Missouri specifics not required beyond 'authorized state program may be more stringent'.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Regional homebuilder based in Marietta, Georgia; 60 employees. Situation: The company is about to clear and grade a 3.5-acre phase of a new subdivision (part of a larger 25-acre common plan of development). Georgia EPD administers the NPDES program and the state erosion and sedimentation law. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Obtain construction stormwater general permit coverage before land disturbance: construction activity disturbing one acre or more (including smaller phases of a larger common plan of development) requires NPDES permit coverage — in Georgia, the EPD-issued construction general permit with a Notice of Intent
expectedObligations.source: Clean Water Act NPDES; EPA 40 CFR 122.26 (construction activity definitions); Georgia EPD construction stormwater general permit (state-administered)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: NOI filed and effective before clearing begins; coverage maintained until final stabilization and Notice of Termination

expectedObligations.requirement: Prepare and implement an erosion, sedimentation and pollution control plan / SWPPP with best management practices (perimeter controls, inlet protection, stabilized construction exit, concrete washout, dewatering controls)
expectedObligations.source: Georgia EPD general permit conditions and the Georgia Erosion and Sedimentation Act (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Plan approved before disturbance; BMPs maintained continuously; plan updated as construction phases change

expectedObligations.requirement: Conduct the permit's self-inspection and monitoring regime (routine inspections on the permit's schedule and after qualifying rain events; in Georgia, sampling/turbidity monitoring requirements per the permit) by qualified/certified personnel
expectedObligations.source: Georgia EPD construction general permit conditions (descriptive; Georgia also requires certified erosion-control personnel under state law — descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-permit inspection frequency plus post-rain-event inspections through final stabilization; records retained on site

expectedObligations.requirement: OH&S obligations of grading work travel with the project (e.g., construction training, equipment safety); if utility trenches exceed 5 feet, excavation protective systems and a competent person are required
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR part 1926 (subpart P for excavations — protective systems generally required at 5 feet or more)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Daily competent-person inspections of excavations; per-phase safety verification

metadata.graderNotes: The applicability trap: 3.5 acres is over one acre on its own, but even a sub-acre phase would still need coverage because it is part of a larger common plan of development — a complete answer states the common-plan rule. Permit coverage must precede disturbance. Georgia specifics (EPD-issued permit, state E&S Act, certified personnel) should be present at least descriptively since the jurisdiction is given; federal-only answers are incomplete but not wrong on framework. The evaluation cadence is project-bounded: inspections until final stabilization, then NOT (register entry retires at Notice of Termination) — credit answers that model the obligation lifecycle. The excavation item tests whether the model remembers construction OH&S rides along; do not require it for a passing grade but weight it favorably.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Data-services company in Ashburn, Virginia; 150 employees at an office/data-center campus. Situation: The company is installing a 750 kW diesel emergency standby generator with a 660-gallon belly tank. The campus already has an 800-gallon heating-oil tank. The generator will run only for outages and for periodic readiness testing/maintenance. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: New stationary compression-ignition engine must comply with the federal New Source Performance Standards: purchase an EPA-certified engine meeting the applicable emission tier, operate and maintain it per requirements, and use the required diesel fuel (ultra-low-sulfur)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 60, subpart IIII (NSPS for stationary compression-ignition internal combustion engines)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Certification documentation verified at purchase/installation; fuel records per delivery; annual compliance evaluation

expectedObligations.requirement: Preserve 'emergency engine' status: non-emergency operation is limited (maintenance and readiness testing within the allowed annual hours — on the order of 100 hours/year); track run hours with a non-resettable hour meter
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 60, subpart IIII emergency-engine provisions (descriptive on exact hour allocations); NESHAP 40 CFR part 63, subpart ZZZZ is generally satisfied for new emergency engines by NSPS compliance (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly run-hour log review; annual verification that testing hours stayed within limits

expectedObligations.requirement: State air permitting or registration for the new engine: Virginia DEQ minor new source requirements/permit exemptions must be checked before installation (a 750 kW emergency generator typically falls under state minor-source or permit-by-rule provisions, not Title V, absent other campus sources)
expectedObligations.source: Clean Air Act minor new source review as implemented by the Virginia DEQ (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time applicability determination and any registration before installation; re-evaluate if additional engines are added (aggregation)

expectedObligations.requirement: SPCC plan now required: aboveground oil storage becomes 660 + 800 = 1,460 gallons, crossing the 1,320-gallon threshold — the belly tank is what tips the facility in (assuming a reasonable expectation of discharge to navigable waters)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Plan before the tank is filled; routine inspections per plan; five-year review

expectedObligations.requirement: Fuel-delivery transfer procedures and spill response for tank filling (an SPCC plan element; also good-practice fire code compliance — descriptive)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (loading/unloading provisions); state/local fire code (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-delivery procedures; annual training briefing

metadata.graderNotes: Two threshold catches drive scoring: (1) the SPCC aggregation — 660 + 800 = 1,460 > 1,320 gallons, so the generator project triggers SPCC even though neither tank alone would; (2) emergency-engine status depends on limiting non-emergency hours (run-hour tracking is the 9.1.2 mechanism). NSPS subpart IIII applies because the engine is new; a model citing only NESHAP ZZZZ for a new engine should note that compliance is generally achieved via IIII. Title V should NOT be asserted for this facility. Watch for: demand-response operation treated as allowed emergency use (risky/limited — hedged treatment is correct); forgetting the existing heating-oil tank; inventing Virginia permit numbers. Bonus (not required): diesel exhaust/CO hazards to nearby air intakes as an OH&S consideration.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Industrial coatings applicator in Elkhart, Indiana; 18 full-time employees; NAICS 332812 (metal coating and allied services). Situation: Annual purchasing records show the facility used about 28,000 pounds of toluene in coatings last calendar year, most of which evaporates during application and curing. The company has never filed toxics release reporting. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Annual Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) reporting for toluene, due July 1: the facility is in a TRI-covered sector (fabricated metals/coating), has 10 or more full-time employee equivalents, and its toluene activity (28,000 lb) exceeds the applicable activity threshold whether classified as 'processed' (25,000 lb) or 'otherwise used' (10,000 lb)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 313; EPA 40 CFR part 372 (TRI)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual threshold determination from purchasing/usage records in Q1; Form R (or eligibility check for Form A) filed by July 1; release estimates re-derived each year

expectedObligations.requirement: Evaluate prior-year filing gaps: the threshold appears to have been exceeded without reporting, so past-year obligations and voluntary disclosure options should be assessed (non-compliance routed to corrective action)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 313 (descriptive; EPA audit policy considerations — descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time look-back determination; document in register with CAPA linkage

expectedObligations.requirement: VOC air emissions from 28,000 lb/yr of evaporating toluene require a state air permitting applicability determination (registration, minor source permit, or exemption per Indiana's air rules)
expectedObligations.source: Clean Air Act as implemented by Indiana's air permitting program (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time determination; ongoing usage tracking against any permit thresholds; monthly VOC purchase log

expectedObligations.requirement: Tier II inventory applicability check for toluene storage quantities on site (10,000 lb threshold at any one time — distinct from the annual-usage TRI thresholds)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 312; EPA 40 CFR part 370 (applicability determination)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Peak on-hand inventory reviewed annually before March 1

expectedObligations.requirement: Employee exposure obligations for toluene (HazCom; exposure assessment against the OSHA PEL)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Exposure assessment on record; annual HazCom audit

metadata.graderNotes: The core discrimination is between three different threshold systems for the same chemical: TRI activity thresholds (25,000 lb processed / 10,000 lb otherwise used — ANNUAL activity), Tier II (10,000 lb PRESENT at any one time), and the OSHA PEL (airborne exposure). The scenario is engineered so TRI applies under either activity classification — an answer need not resolve processed-vs-otherwise-used, but must not confuse TRI with Tier II. Employee-count test: 18 full-time employees ≥ 10 FTE, covered NAICS — both prongs must be checked, not assumed. The look-back/non-filing point tests whether the model connects the register to compliance-evaluation findings and CAPA (per the LegalLedger handoff design). Watch for: 'toluene evaporates so nothing is released' (evaporative emissions ARE reportable releases); claiming TRI is quarterly; July 1 deadline wrong.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Convenience store operator in Las Cruces, New Mexico; 15 employees across two stores. Situation: The company is replacing two aging 10,000-gallon gasoline underground storage tanks at one store with new double-walled tanks, and permanently closing the old ones. New Mexico administers a state UST program. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: New tanks must meet UST performance standards: spill prevention (spill buckets), overfill prevention, corrosion protection, and release detection from day one; notify/register the new systems with the state program before or upon installation per state procedure
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 280 (as implemented by the New Mexico state UST program)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Installation verification and registration at commissioning; release-detection results reviewed monthly

expectedObligations.requirement: Permanent closure of the old tanks: empty and clean, close per required methods (removal or approved in-place closure), conduct a site assessment for contamination, and notify the implementing agency within the required advance window; report and address any discovered releases
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 280 (closure and release response subparts, state-administered)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time closure process with documented site assessment; contingent release-response obligations if contamination is found

expectedObligations.requirement: Ongoing operation and maintenance: designated Class A/B/C operators trained per requirements; periodic walkthrough inspections (30-day cycle) and periodic equipment testing (e.g., annual release-detection equipment test, spill bucket and overfill testing on the required multi-year cycles)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 280 (operator training and 2015 O&M provisions — descriptive on exact test intervals)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: 30-day walkthroughs; annual and multi-year test calendar tracked in the register; operator-training records reviewed annually

expectedObligations.requirement: Financial responsibility for taking corrective action and compensating third parties for UST releases (state fund participation and/or insurance per New Mexico program)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 280 financial responsibility provisions (descriptive; state fund mechanics vary)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Coverage verified annually and at each renewal

expectedObligations.requirement: Worker safety during tank removal (contractor operation): excavation protection, flammable-atmosphere control, and contractor-management duties for the store operator
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR part 1926 (excavation subpart P; contractor's obligations) and OSH Act 5(a)(1) for host duties — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Pre-job contractor verification; project-duration site checks

metadata.graderNotes: Complete answers cover the full lifecycle: new-system standards + registration, closure with site assessment (the most-missed element — closure is not just pulling tanks), the O&M cadence (30-day walkthroughs, annual/multi-year testing — this maps directly onto 9.1.2), operator training A/B/C, and financial responsibility. State administration should be acknowledged (New Mexico program, possible state fund). The contractor-safety item is a ride-along; credit but do not require detail. Watch for: applying the 42,000-gallon SPCC underground threshold here (SPCC generally defers to part 280-regulated USTs — conflating SPCC and UST programs is an error); missing the release-response contingency if the site assessment finds contamination.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Rural water utility near Cullman, Alabama; 20 employees. Situation: The treatment plant stores chlorine in 150-pound cylinders, typically 1,200 pounds total on site. Last night a valve failure released an estimated 25 pounds of chlorine gas over about an hour before operators isolated the cylinder; no injuries, but a nearby road was briefly closed. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register — including reporting duties already triggered and any thresholds NOT crossed. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: The release exceeded chlorine's 10-pound reportable quantity: immediate notification to the National Response Center was required under CERCLA
expectedObligations.source: CERCLA Section 103; EPA 40 CFR part 302 (chlorine RQ = 10 lb)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Event-triggered (immediate); post-incident verification that notification was made and documented

expectedObligations.requirement: EPCRA release notification: immediate notice to the State Emergency Response Commission and Local Emergency Planning Committee (chlorine is an EHS and the release left the facility), followed by a written follow-up emergency notice
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 304; EPA 40 CFR part 355
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Event-triggered; follow-up report tracked to completion; notification procedure tested annually

expectedObligations.requirement: Ongoing emergency-planning status: chlorine's Threshold Planning Quantity is 100 pounds, and 1,200 pounds is routinely on site, so the facility is (and should already have been) subject to EPCRA 302 planning coordination with the LEPC and Tier II reporting (EHS threshold: lower of 500 lb or the TPQ, i.e., 100 lb)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Sections 302 and 312; EPA 40 CFR parts 355 and 370
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Verify the 302 designation and current Tier II filing now; annual March 1 Tier II cycle; re-notify on quantity changes

expectedObligations.requirement: OSHA Process Safety Management does NOT apply: PSM's threshold quantity for chlorine is 1,500 pounds and the site holds 1,200 pounds — register as evaluated-not-applicable with a re-check trigger on inventory increases
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (Appendix A threshold for chlorine: 1,500 lb)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Inventory-change-triggered re-evaluation; annual confirmation

expectedObligations.requirement: EPA Risk Management Program does NOT apply: the RMP threshold for chlorine is 2,500 pounds — but the Clean Air Act Section 112(r)(1) general duty to prevent and mitigate accidental releases applies regardless, as does the OSH Act General Duty Clause for employee exposure
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 68 (chlorine TQ 2,500 lb); CAA Section 112(r)(1); OSH Act Section 5(a)(1)
