expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Applicability re-checked on inventory change; general-duty prevention measures evaluated annually

expectedObligations.requirement: If the utility's own employees respond to chlorine releases, emergency-response training and procedures apply (HAZWOPER emergency response provisions), including respiratory protection for response
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Training currency verified annually; post-incident critique after each response

metadata.graderNotes: Four-threshold discrimination on one chemical: RQ 10 lb (crossed — CERCLA/NRC and EPCRA 304 both fire), TPQ 100 lb (long since crossed by storage — 302 planning and Tier II at the 100 lb EHS threshold), PSM TQ 1,500 lb (NOT crossed at 1,200 lb), RMP TQ 2,500 lb (NOT crossed). A passing answer gets the two 'applies' and two 'does not apply' calls right AND notes the general-duty backstops (CAA 112(r)(1), OSH Act 5(a)(1)). The most common failure: asserting PSM/RMP apply because chlorine is dangerous, or missing the immediate-notification duties already triggered. Also credit: register entries for not-applicable items retained with re-check triggers (LegalLedger register design); water-system-specific state notification duties (descriptive). The 1910.120(q) item distinguishes strong answers.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Precision machine shop in Erie, Pennsylvania; 30 employees; a very small quantity generator (VSQG) normally generating about 40 kg/month of hazardous waste. Situation: The shop plans a one-time decommissioning and cleanout of an old vapor degreaser containing trichloroethylene (TCE); the cleanout will generate roughly 1,600 kg of TCE still bottoms and spent solvent in a single month, then generation returns to normal. Pennsylvania DEP administers an authorized RCRA program. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazardous waste determination: spent TCE from degreasing is a listed halogenated spent solvent (F001); still bottoms from its recovery are also regulated
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 261 (F001 spent solvent listing); determination duty under 40 CFR part 262
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time determination documented before the cleanout

expectedObligations.requirement: Without special provisions, generating 1,600 kg in one month would make the shop a Large Quantity Generator for that month (over 1,000 kg/month), with full LQG conditions; however, the episodic generation provisions allow a VSQG to maintain its category for a planned episodic event by notifying the state in advance (at least 30 days), obtaining an EPA ID number, managing the waste per the episodic conditions, and moving it off site within the allowed period
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262, subpart L (episodic generation) — as adopted by the authorized state program
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Advance notification tracked; waste shipped within the episodic window (60 days); one planned event per calendar year — event calendar tracked in the register

expectedObligations.requirement: Confirm Pennsylvania has adopted the episodic generation provisions (authorized states must be checked; if not adopted, the shop must comply with the higher generator category for that month)
expectedObligations.source: State-authorized RCRA program status (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time verification with PA DEP before scheduling the event

expectedObligations.requirement: Manifest the shipment with a registered hazardous waste transporter to a designated facility; land disposal restriction notifications accompany the waste
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262, subpart B (manifest); 40 CFR part 268 (land disposal restrictions) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Per-shipment; manifest copies reconciled on return

expectedObligations.requirement: Worker protection during the cleanout: TCE has a specific OSHA substance standard consideration (PEL under Z-tables), and tank entry may constitute permit-required confined space entry with LOTO
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1000 (TCE PEL); 29 CFR 1910.146 and 29 CFR 1910.147 if entry is required
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Pre-job hazard assessment and permits; post-job review

metadata.graderNotes: The center of gravity is the episodic-generation reasoning: (1) recognize that 1,600 kg in one month means LQG for that month by default (NOT SQG — over 1,000 kg is LQG; answers saying 'becomes an SQG' fail the threshold logic); (2) know that the Generator Improvements Rule's episodic provisions can preserve VSQG status for a planned event with 30-day advance notice, EPA ID, and timely shipment; (3) flag state adoption as a check, since authorized states adopt at different times. F001 identification matters (TCE degreasing is the canonical F001). The OH&S ride-along (confined space/LOTO for tank cleanout, TCE exposure) marks a strong answer. Grader note: verify the episodic-event details (30-day notice, 60-day removal, one planned event/year) against current 40 CFR part 262 subpart L text.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Electronics hardware manufacturer in Warren, Michigan; 130 employees. Situation: The company is adding an in-house decorative chromium and nickel electroplating line, including acid pickling, plating tanks, rinse cascades, and an on-site wastewater pretreatment system that will discharge to the municipal sewer (POTW) and produce a filter-press sludge. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Wastewater treatment sludge from electroplating operations is listed hazardous waste F006; generating it changes the facility's hazardous waste profile and generator category must be re-determined (accumulation, manifesting, reporting per category)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 261 (F006 listing) and 40 CFR part 262 (generator standards)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Waste determination before first sludge generation; monthly generation counting; category-driven inspection and reporting cadence

expectedObligations.requirement: Pretreatment obligations for discharge to the POTW: categorical effluent standards for metal finishing plus the POTW's local limits and an industrial user permit/authorization from the POTW, with self-monitoring and reporting per the permit
expectedObligations.source: Clean Water Act pretreatment program: EPA 40 CFR part 403 (general pretreatment) and 40 CFR part 433 (metal finishing categorical standards)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Permit obtained before discharge; self-monitoring/sampling and periodic compliance reports per permit schedule (commonly semiannual, permit-specific)

expectedObligations.requirement: Air toxics requirements for chromium electroplating: the NESHAP for chromium electroplating and anodizing applies (including decorative chromium), requiring emission limits or management practices such as fume suppressants/controls, initial notification and compliance demonstrations, and ongoing monitoring/recordkeeping; state air permitting applicability must also be determined
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 63, subpart N (chromium electroplating/anodizing NESHAP); state minor-source air permitting (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Initial notification and compliance demonstration at startup; ongoing surface-tension/parameter monitoring and records per the subpart; annual compliance certification per permit

expectedObligations.requirement: Hexavalent chromium worker-exposure obligations: initial exposure determination against the Cr(VI) action level (2.5 µg/m3) and PEL (5 µg/m3), engineering controls, regulated areas/hygiene as triggered, medical surveillance per the standard's triggers
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Baseline exposure determination at startup; periodic monitoring per the standard; annual program review

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazard communication and PPE for plating chemicals (chromic acid, nickel salts, acids): SDSs, labeling, training, certified PPE hazard assessment, eyewash/shower availability for corrosives
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Before startup; quarterly area inspections; annual HazCom/PPE review

expectedObligations.requirement: EPCRA inventory and release reporting applicability: plating-bath acids and metal compounds may trigger Tier II (including EHS thresholds for some acids) and TRI reporting for chromium/nickel compounds (which carry TRI reporting obligations; certain metal categories have specific threshold treatments)
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Sections 311/312/313; EPA 40 CFR parts 370 and 372 (applicability determination)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Initial applicability determination at startup; annual Tier II (March 1) and TRI (July 1) threshold reviews

metadata.graderNotes: This is the flagship mixed scenario; a complete answer must span at least: F006 (the canonical plating listing — its absence is a major miss), pretreatment (part 403 + part 433 categorical standards + POTW permit), the chromium electroplating NESHAP (subpart N applies to decorative chrome too), and 1910.1026 with correct AL/PEL numbers. HazCom/PPE/eyewash and EPCRA applicability round it out. Both ISO 14001 6.1.3 AND 45001 6.1.3 mappings are required — an answer mapping everything to one standard fails the framing. Watch for: claiming discharge to sewer needs an NPDES permit (it needs pretreatment/industrial-user authorization, not a direct-discharge NPDES permit); missing the sludge entirely; PSM assertions (typical decorative plating chemicals are not PSM-listed at these scales — hedged treatment acceptable). Grader should verify subpart N's coverage details for decorative chromium and the current compliance-demonstration specifics.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Custom woodworking shop in Durango, Colorado; 9 employees (peak 9 last year). Inventory audit: about 300 gallons total of finishes, stains, and oils (three 55-gallon drums, the rest in 1-5 gallon containers); maximum chemical on hand about 2,000 pounds of any one product; roughly 50 kg/month of hazardous waste (spent solvent, finish waste). Situation: A consultant's proposal claims the shop needs an SPCC plan, Tier II reports, a full LQG hazardous waste program, and complete OSHA 300 recordkeeping, quoting $30,000 to implement. Ask: Evaluate each claimed obligation and identify what actually applies. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company (including non-applicability with basis), the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: SPCC plan NOT required: aggregate aboveground OIL storage counting only containers of 55 gallons and larger is about 165 gallons (three drums) — far below the 1,320-gallon threshold; finishes/stains count only to the extent they are oils, and the small containers do not count
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (applicability)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual re-verification of oil container inventory; re-evaluate on any bulk tank purchase

expectedObligations.requirement: Tier II reporting NOT required: no hazardous chemical reaches the 10,000-pound threshold (max ~2,000 lb) and no Extremely Hazardous Substance is present at or above its lower EHS threshold on the facts given
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Section 312; EPA 40 CFR part 370 (applicability)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Annual peak-inventory review before March 1; re-evaluate on inventory growth or new EHS chemicals

expectedObligations.requirement: LQG program NOT required — the shop is a VSQG at ~50 kg/month (≤100 kg/month): conditions are waste identification, accumulation limits (no more than 1,000 kg on site to preserve VSQG status), and delivery to an authorized/permitted facility; no manifest, contingency plan, biennial report, or formal training program is federally required at VSQG
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR 262.14 (VSQG conditions); category thresholds at 40 CFR part 262 — Colorado's state program may be more stringent (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly generation counting to confirm category; annual review; state-rule check once

expectedObligations.requirement: OSHA 300/301/300A recordkeeping NOT required: 9 employees peak in the prior calendar year is within the 10-or-fewer partial exemption — but severe-injury REPORTING (fatality 8 hours; hospitalization/amputation/eye loss 24 hours) still applies
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.1 (exemption) and 29 CFR 1904.39 (reporting still applies)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Headcount re-verified each January; reporting procedure verified annually

expectedObligations.requirement: What DOES apply and should anchor the register: hazard communication (29 CFR 1910.1200), machine guarding (29 CFR 1910.212), PPE hazard assessment (29 CFR 1910.132), spray/flammable finishing controls if spraying (29 CFR 1910.107, 1910.106), portable fire extinguisher inspections (29 CFR 1910.157), wood dust housekeeping and combustible dust control via the General Duty Clause (OSH Act 5(a)(1))
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910 (as cited); OSH Act Section 5(a)(1)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Monthly extinguisher visual checks and annual maintenance; quarterly housekeeping/guarding inspections; annual HazCom and PPE review

metadata.graderNotes: Pure applicability-reasoning item; the correct verdict is that ALL FOUR consultant claims are wrong on the facts (SPCC no, Tier II no, LQG no — VSQG yes with light conditions, 300-log no — but 1904.39 reporting yes), while a real set of OH&S obligations does apply. Scoring: each of the four rejections requires the correct threshold and arithmetic (165 countable oil gallons vs 1,320; 2,000 lb vs 10,000; 50 kg vs 100/1,000 kg tiers; 9 employees vs 10). Register philosophy matters: not-applicable entries stay in the register with basis and re-check triggers (headcount, inventory, waste-rate changes). Watch for: models deferring to the consultant; counting the 1-5 gallon containers toward SPCC; conflating VSQG accumulation cap (1,000 kg) with the monthly rate; forgetting that severe-injury reporting survives the recordkeeping exemption.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Specialty chemicals distributor headquartered in Houston, Texas, with warehouses in Texas and New Jersey; 220 employees; repackages and distributes industrial chemicals. Situation: OSHA published a final rule updating the Hazard Communication Standard (aligning 29 CFR 1910.1200 with a newer revision of the UN GHS), with phased compliance dates for substances and mixtures over the coming years. The regulatory-change feed flagged it. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this regulatory change creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register, and how the register itself must respond. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: Register maintenance duty: ISO 45001 6.1.3 requires determining and keeping up to date the legal and other requirements — the amended HazCom rule must be entered as a change to the existing 1910.1200 register entries, with affected processes, sites, and roles identified and compliance-date milestones recorded
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (as amended, 2024 final rule); ISO 45001 6.1.3 up-to-date requirement (framing, not verbatim)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Register updated within the organization's regulatory-change SLA; evaluation milestones set at each phased compliance date

expectedObligations.requirement: As a distributor/repackager: reclassify hazards and update labels and SDSs for shipped containers to the amended criteria and formats by the applicable substance and mixture compliance dates (distributor-specific shipping deadlines follow the manufacturer/importer dates in the rule)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (classification, labels, SDS duties of manufacturers/importers/distributors, as amended)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Milestone-based evaluation before each compliance date: sample-based label/SDS audits per product family; full conformance verification at each deadline

expectedObligations.requirement: As an employer: update the written HazCom program, workplace labeling, and employee training to cover new or changed label elements and SDS format changes at both warehouses
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (employer duties, as amended)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Training on new elements completed by the applicable employer-facing dates; annual HazCom audit updated to the new criteria

expectedObligations.requirement: Small-container labeling provisions in the amended rule may relieve or change duties for repackaged small containers — an applicability determination for the repackaging lines is required
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (amended small-container label provisions) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time determination per packaging line; verify at first post-change label run

expectedObligations.requirement: State-plan check: the New Jersey warehouse is under federal OSHA for private employers, but any state right-to-know or labeling overlays should be re-verified as part of the change assessment (descriptive)
expectedObligations.source: State right-to-know laws (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time verification during the change assessment

metadata.graderNotes: This item tests the regulatory-change WORKFLOW, not chemistry: the register entry for 1910.1200 must be versioned/updated, impacted obligations re-linked to processes and sites, and 9.1.2 evaluations scheduled against the rule's phased compliance dates (substances first, mixtures later — dates span roughly 2026-2028). Grader: verify the exact compliance dates from the 2024 final rule; a model should either state them correctly or hedge — confidently wrong dates are penalized. The distributor-vs-employer duality is the second axis: shipped-container/SDS duties vs workplace program/training duties — an answer covering only the employer side is half-complete. Watch for: models treating this as a brand-new obligation rather than a change to an existing register entry; inventing a GHS revision number without hedging; missing the milestone-based evaluation cadence.

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Furniture manufacturer in Hickory, North Carolina; 75 employees. Situation: The company is installing a new enclosed spray-finishing booth for solvent-borne lacquers and sealers; projected coating usage implies roughly 8 tons per year of VOC emissions potential. The change adds spray operations, flammable liquid storage, spent solvent and lacquer waste, and used booth filters. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this situation creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: State air permitting applicability determination before construction: ~8 tons/yr VOC typically lands in state minor-source/registration territory (North Carolina DAQ), and wood-furniture surface-coating air toxics rules must be checked for applicability; permit or exemption documented before the booth operates
expectedObligations.source: Clean Air Act minor new source review as implemented by the state (descriptive); EPA wood furniture surface-coating NESHAP applicability check (descriptive — major-source-dependent)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time pre-construction determination; monthly coating/VOC usage log against any permit limits; annual emissions statement per state requirements

expectedObligations.requirement: Spray-finishing safety: booth construction, ventilation, ignition source control, residue management, and no-smoking provisions
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.107
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Booth verification at commissioning; monthly filter/deposit inspections

expectedObligations.requirement: Flammable liquids storage and handling for lacquers/solvents (cabinets, quantity limits, bonding/grounding for transfers)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Storage verified at rollout; monthly fire-safety inspections

expectedObligations.requirement: Respiratory protection and PPE for sprayers pending exposure assessment; hazard communication updates for the new coatings
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Exposure assessment at startup; annual fit testing if respirators required; annual HazCom audit

expectedObligations.requirement: Hazardous waste determinations for spent solvents (F003/F005 listings are typical for lacquer solvents such as acetone/toluene/MEK blends, plus D001 ignitability), waste coatings, and booth filters; recount generator category with the new waste streams
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR parts 261 and 262
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Determinations before first disposal; monthly generation counting; category-driven cadence thereafter

expectedObligations.requirement: Solvent-contaminated wipes/rags may qualify for the conditional exclusions from hazardous waste (accumulation, container, labeling, and no-free-liquids conditions) — an applicability determination that reduces burden if the conditions are met
expectedObligations.source: EPA solvent-contaminated wipes conditional exclusion (40 CFR part 261 provisions) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time determination; monthly verification of exclusion conditions

metadata.graderNotes: Balanced mixed scenario: the answer must carry both chains — OH&S (1910.107 booth, 1910.106 flammables, respirators/HazCom) and environmental (air permitting determination BEFORE construction, waste determinations with F003/F005 + D001, wipes exclusion). Pre-construction timing on the air side is a key correctness point (permit-then-build, not build-then-permit). The wood-furniture NESHAP is major-source dependent — expected treatment is a hedged applicability check, not assertion. Watch for: Title V claims at 8 tpy (wrong absent other large sources); mapping the booth safety items to 14001; forgetting booth filters as a waste stream; asserting specific F-listings without knowing the actual solvent constituents (hedged listing logic is acceptable and preferred).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Packaging manufacturer headquartered in Dayton, Ohio; 400 employees company-wide. Situation: The company just closed the acquisition of a corrugated-packaging plant in Tacoma, Washington (180 employees). The Tacoma plant holds a state air operating permit (synthetic minor), is a Large Quantity Generator of hazardous waste, files Tier II annually, and has an industrial stormwater permit. Washington runs its own OSHA-approved state plan (DOSH) and its own authorized environmental programs. The corporate register was built for Ohio (federal OSHA) sites. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations the acquisition creates or affects and how the register must be restructured. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: OH&S register re-baseline: Washington is a state-plan state — the Tacoma plant is regulated by Washington DOSH under state rules (WAC), which can differ from and exceed federal OSHA; the register's OSHA citations must be swapped/verified for Washington equivalents
expectedObligations.source: Washington State Plan (DOSH; Washington Administrative Code) — descriptive
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time re-baseline within the integration window; ongoing Washington regulatory-change monitoring

expectedObligations.requirement: Ownership-change notifications and permit updates: air operating permit (transfer/ownership-change notice to the state permitting authority), industrial stormwater permit (permittee/NOI update), and hazardous waste Site ID form update for the ownership change (EPA Form 8700-12)
expectedObligations.source: State air and water permit transfer provisions (descriptive); EPA 40 CFR part 262 (Site ID notification for LQG ownership/contact changes)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: One-time filings within each program's required window after closing; confirmation letters tracked in the register

expectedObligations.requirement: Continuity of the acquired plant's ongoing obligations without gap: LQG conditions (90-day accumulation, weekly inspections, contingency plan updated with new owner/emergency contacts, biennial report), Tier II (update facility ownership/contact information; next March 1 filing), synthetic-minor permit limits (emissions caps that keep the plant below major-source thresholds must keep being met and monitored)
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 262 (LQG); EPCRA Section 312 / 40 CFR part 370; state air operating permit conditions (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: No-gap verification at closing; then each obligation's native cadence (weekly inspections, annual Tier II, permit monitoring/reporting schedule)

expectedObligations.requirement: SPCC and stormwater plan updates: facility plans (SPCC plan if applicable, SWPPP) must be updated for the new owner/management structure and re-signed/re-certified as the plan provisions require
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 112 (plan amendments — descriptive on amendment type); stormwater general permit SWPPP conditions (descriptive)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Plan updates during integration; then native review cycles (SPCC five-year review; SWPPP annual review)

expectedObligations.requirement: Baseline evaluation of compliance for the acquired site: a full initial 9.1.2 evaluation of the inherited register (permits, waste, reporting, OH&S programs) to establish compliance status under new ownership, with findings routed to corrective action
expectedObligations.source: ISO 14001 / ISO 45001 9.1.2 (evaluation process — framing); due-diligence follow-through (descriptive)
expectedObligations.isoMapping: ISO 14001 6.1.3 and ISO 45001 6.1.3 (register consolidation), evaluated via 9.1.2
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Baseline evaluation within a defined window post-closing (e.g., 90 days); then per-obligation cadences; first integrated management-review input at next cycle

metadata.graderNotes: Integration-architecture item. Four required moves: (1) state-plan recognition — Washington DOSH/WAC replaces federal OSHA citations (an answer applying 29 CFR to Tacoma as the operative source misses the point; federal references as 'at least as effective as' context is fine); (2) ownership-change notifications across programs (air permit transfer, stormwater permittee update, RCRA Site ID update); (3) no-gap continuity of LQG/Tier II/synthetic-minor obligations with their native cadences; (4) a baseline 9.1.2 evaluation of the acquired register with CAPA routing. Synthetic-minor status is a subtle test: the emissions caps are what keep the plant out of Title V, so exceeding them post-acquisition is a real risk worth naming. Watch for: treating the acquisition as creating brand-new permits (they transfer/update, not reissue from scratch — program-specific, hedged treatment fine); ignoring Washington's authorized/more-stringent environmental programs (e.g., state dangerous-waste rules are broader than federal RCRA — credit if mentioned).

tasks.prompt: Company profile: Cold-storage and food logistics operator in Grand Island, Nebraska; 90 employees. Situation: The company is expanding its anhydrous ammonia refrigeration system from 8,000 pounds to approximately 14,000 pounds of ammonia charge to serve a new freezer wing. The company already files Tier II for the ammonia and coordinates with the LEPC. Ask: Identify the compliance obligations this expansion creates or affects for the compliance-obligations register. For each obligation: state the requirement, its source, its applicability to this company, the ISO clause it maps to (ISO 14001 6.1.3 / ISO 45001 6.1.3), and how and when compliance should be evaluated (9.1.2).

expectedObligations.requirement: OSHA Process Safety Management now applies: anhydrous ammonia's PSM threshold quantity is 10,000 pounds, and the expansion crosses it — a full PSM program is required (process safety information, process hazard analysis, operating procedures, training, mechanical integrity, management of change, pre-startup safety review, incident investigation, emergency planning, compliance audits)
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (Appendix A: anhydrous ammonia TQ 10,000 lb)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Program in place at/before crossing the threshold; PHA revalidated at least every five years; compliance audits at least every three years; MOC on every process change; mechanical-integrity inspections per program schedule

expectedObligations.requirement: EPA Risk Management Program now applies: ammonia's RMP threshold is also 10,000 pounds — develop and submit a Risk Management Plan (likely Program 3 given PSM coverage), including hazard assessment with worst-case release analysis, prevention program, and emergency response coordination
expectedObligations.source: EPA 40 CFR part 68 (anhydrous ammonia TQ 10,000 lb)
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: RMP submitted before exceeding the threshold quantity in the process; plan updated and resubmitted at least every five years and on qualifying changes; coordination with local responders per the rule's cadence

expectedObligations.requirement: Existing EPCRA obligations continue and must be updated for the new quantity: ammonia is an EHS (TPQ 500 lb — long since exceeded), so Section 302 planning coordination and Tier II reporting (EHS threshold 500 lb) continue with updated quantities and system details
expectedObligations.source: EPCRA Sections 302/312; EPA 40 CFR parts 355 and 370
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: LEPC notified of the significant change; Tier II updated at the next March 1 filing; re-verify at further inventory changes

expectedObligations.requirement: Release-reporting readiness: ammonia's reportable quantity is 100 pounds — CERCLA/NRC and EPCRA 304 notification procedures must be scaled to the larger system and drilled
expectedObligations.source: CERCLA Section 103 / EPA 40 CFR part 302 (ammonia RQ 100 lb); EPCRA Section 304 / 40 CFR part 355
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Procedure verified now; annual notification drill; event-triggered execution

expectedObligations.requirement: Emergency response posture for employees: decide response-vs-evacuate strategy; if employees will respond to ammonia releases, HAZWOPER emergency response training, an emergency response plan, and respiratory protection apply
expectedObligations.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120(q); 29 CFR 1910.134; CAA Section 112(r)(1) general duty as backstop
expectedObligations.evaluationCadence: Training currency annually; drills per plan; post-incident critiques

metadata.graderNotes: The crux: 8,000 → 14,000 lb crosses BOTH the OSHA PSM and EPA RMP thresholds (both 10,000 lb for anhydrous ammonia) — a passing answer must catch both, and the strongest answers note the register previously (correctly) carried PSM/RMP as evaluated-not-applicable at 8,000 lb and now flips them. Program 3 RMP follows from PSM coverage. The layered cadences are the 9.1.2 payoff: PHA 5-year revalidation, PSM audit 3-year, RMP 5-year resubmission, Tier II annual, MOC continuous — credit answers that lay out this calendar. Existing EPCRA duties (302/Tier II at the 500-lb EHS threshold) were already active and must not be presented as new. Watch for: only citing one of PSM/RMP; wrong TQs; claiming ammonia refrigeration is exempt from PSM (industry petitions notwithstanding, covered processes over TQ are in scope — hedged discussion of enforcement policy acceptable); ignoring the response-vs-evacuate decision that determines 1910.120(q) applicability.
